slide_text: Dictionaries A dictionary maps keys to values — like an index at the back of a book. You look up a key in O(1) time, regardless of how many entries exist. In this chapter you will use dictionaries to: Count word frequencies in text Group words that are anagrams of each other Track and query expenses by category Navigate: press or Space to advance | to go back

Part 2: Anagrams Two words are anagrams of each other if they contain exactly the same letters (in possibly different order). Examples: "listen" and "silent" are anagrams. Part 5: Inventing Hashing (Why Dicts Are Fast) You've used dictionaries all chapter without asking the awkward question: is instant even if holds a million keys. A list would have to check entries one by one. How does a dict jump straight to the right spot? The answer is an idea you're about to invent: turn the key into a number , and use that number as a position.

Letters Are Already Numbers Python exposes each character's numeric code: is , and goes back to . Write returning the position of a lowercase letter in the alphabet — → 0, → 1, ... → 25 — using (no lookup tables!).

A Number for Any String One letter is easy. For a whole string, the simplest recipe: add up the character codes . That gives a big number; to turn it into a position , take the remainder when dividing by the number of slots available. Write = (sum of of every character) . The result is always a valid index between and — exactly what you need to pick a slot in a list of buckets. [code block]

The Collision Run this before reading on: [code block] Both give . Of course — they're anagrams (Part 2 of this chapter!), so they contain the same letters, and addition doesn't care about order. Two different keys landing in the same bucket is called a collision , and a hash that collides for every anagram is a bad hash. The fix: make position matter. Weight each character by where it sits: Write using the weighted sum (hint: ), and confirm the anagram pair now separates. [code block]

The Same Trick at Data-Center Scale You just invented how a dict works inside: Hash the key to a bucket index — one arithmetic step, no searching. Go directly to that bucket. Collisions are unavoidable (infinitely many strings, finitely many buckets), so each bucket keeps a short list to check — a few items, not a million. That's why costs the same whether the dict holds ten keys or ten million: this is what O(1) lookup means. Now zoom out. A big website can't fit a billion users on one database server; it splits them across many. Which server holds user ? Same invention: hash the key. With numeric IDs the hash is just the remainder. Write returning , then check the test's fairness experiment: hashing 10,000 users across 7 servers should load every server almost equally. [code block] Think about it (no code): if you add an 8th server, becomes — which users are now on the wrong server? (Almost all of them! Real systems soften this with consistent hashing — worth a web search. Python dicts face the same event when they grow: they resize and re-hash every key.)

What Happens on a Collision? You built a hash function that converts a string to a number, then uses modulo to pick a bucket. What happens when two different keys hash to the same bucket (a collision)? A. The second key silently replaces the first — data is lost B. Python raises an error and refuses to insert C. The bucket stores both key-value pairs, and lookup checks each one — O(1) on average if collisions are rare D. The hash function automatically picks a different bucket
